title: Query Anagrams
statement:
A feed runs a daily word-puzzle post: users see a scrambled set of letters and guess the word. Before a puzzle goes live, the backend checks how many dictionary words each scramble could be.

Write def solution(words, queries). words is the dictionary and queries is a list of scrambles. Return a list of integers, one per query in order: the number of entries in words that are anagrams of that query.

  • Two strings are anagrams when they use the same letters with the same counts ("aab" and "aba" are; "aab" and "abb" are not).
  • A word equal to the query counts.
  • Duplicate entries in words count separately.

examples.why: inlets rearranges to listen, silent, enlist and tinsel. google matches itself. Nothing matches banana.
The duplicate "abc" counts twice. "ab" is not an anagram of "cba" (different length).
Same letters is not enough: the counts must match. "aba" has two a and matches only "aab".

constraints: all strings contain only lowercase English letters

think.q: What counts as a match, and what do you return?
think.a: A word matches a query when it has exactly the same multiset of letters: same length, same count of each letter. Return one count per query, in query order. A word equal to the query counts, and duplicate words count twice.

think.q: Sort the letters of each word in example 2.
think.a: abc, bca, abc, cab all become "abc"; ab becomes "ab". So the groups are {"abc": 4, "ab": 1}. Query cba sorts to "abc": 4. Query abcd sorts to "abcd": not there, 0.

think.q: What is the first idea that works?
think.a: For each query, loop over every word and compare sorted(w) == sorted(q). That is Q × W comparisons: 10^8 at the limits, far too slow, and it re-sorts every word Q times.

Hashing with a canonical key. Map every word to a key that is equal for all its anagrams: the sorted letters, or a tuple of 26 letter counts. Count keys once in a dict, then each query is one key computation plus one lookup.

1. Define key(word) = "".join(sorted(word)).
  2. groups = Counter(key(w) for w in words).
  3. For each query, append groups[key(q)] (a Counter returns 0 for a missing key).
  4. Return the list.

Empty words (every answer is 0). Empty queries (return []). Duplicate words. Same letters with different counts ("aab" vs "abb"). Different lengths that share letters ("ab" vs "abc"). Single-letter strings. Repeated queries.

hints: You answer many queries against one fixed dictionary. Do the expensive work on the dictionary once.
Find a key that is the same for every anagram of a word and different otherwise. Sorting the letters gives one.
Count keys with Counter(key(w) for w in words). Then the answer to a query is just groups[key(q)].
explain:
Example 1: the keys are listen → eilnst, silent → eilnst, enlist → eilnst, google → eggloo, tinsel → eilnst. So groups = {"eilnst": 4, "eggloo": 1}.

  • inlets → eilnst → 4.
  • google → eggloo → 1.
  • banana → aaabnn → 0.

Building the groups costs O(W · L log L) once; each query then costs O(L log L) for its sort plus O(L) to hash the key. An alternative key is a tuple of 26 counts, tuple(counts) where counts[ord(ch) - 97] += 1: O(L + 26) per word with no sort. For words of at most 20 letters the sorted string is shorter to write and in practice as fast, because sorted runs in C.
complexity: O((W + Q) · L log L) time, O(W · L) extra space for the key counts

talk: Precompute once: the dictionary is fixed and queries are many, so I pay O(W · L log L) once and each query is O(L log L) plus one dict lookup, instead of O(W · L log L) per query.
Canonical key: "".join(sorted(word)). I join to a string because a list is not hashable; tuple(sorted(word)) also works.
The other key is a 26-count tuple: O(L) per word with no sort. It wins when words are long; for short words the sorted string is simpler and sorted runs in C.
Counter handles both duplicates (each word adds 1) and missing keys (lookup returns 0 without inserting), so there is no special case for either.
Edge cases: empty dictionary, empty query list, same letters with different counts, and different lengths that share letters.
extensions: Return the matching words themselves, grouped, instead of counts (LC 49 Group Anagrams). What do you store per key?
The dictionary changes between queries (add and remove words). What does each update cost with your structure?
Count dictionary words that can be built from the query's letters, using each letter at most as often as it appears (a "sub-anagram"). Why does one hash key no longer work?
Strings can contain any Unicode character, not just a to z. Which key still works?
The dictionary has 100 million words and does not fit on one machine. How do you shard it so a query hits one shard?
